name: Quick Ratio (Acid-Test)
description: Computes the quick (acid-test) ratio as current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities. It measures a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using only its most liquid assets, excluding inventory that may be slow to convert to cash.
notes: Inventory is subtracted because it is the least liquid current asset; a stricter version also removes prepaid expenses. A ratio near or above 1 is generally considered healthy.

name: Operating Profit Margin
description: Computes the operating profit margin as operating income divided by revenue. It shows the proportion of each sales dollar remaining after covering operating expenses but before interest and taxes, reflecting core operating profitability.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). It excludes interest and taxes, so it isolates operating performance from financing and tax effects.

name: Net Profit Margin (Return on Sales)
description: Computes the net profit margin as net income divided by revenue. It measures the share of each sales dollar that becomes bottom-line profit after all expenses, including interest and taxes, have been deducted.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Unlike operating margin, it includes interest, taxes, and any non-operating items.

name: Inventory Turnover Ratio
description: Computes inventory turnover as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. It indicates how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory over a period, reflecting how efficiently stock is managed.
notes: Use cost of goods sold (not sales) in the numerator and average inventory over the period; dividing 365 by this ratio gives average days inventory is held.

name: Receivables Turnover Ratio
description: Computes receivables turnover as net credit sales divided by average accounts receivable. It shows how many times a firm collects its average receivables during a period, indicating the effectiveness of credit and collection policies.
notes: Ideally the numerator is credit sales only, excluding cash sales; dividing 365 by this ratio gives the average collection period in days.

name: Total Asset Turnover
description: Computes total asset turnover as revenue divided by total assets. It measures how efficiently a company uses its entire asset base to generate sales, expressing sales produced per unit of assets.
notes: Often total assets is taken as an average of beginning and ending balances. A higher value means assets are used more efficiently, though typical levels vary widely by industry.

name: DuPont Identity (3-Step ROE)
description: Decomposes return on equity into the product of net profit margin, asset turnover, and the equity multiplier. This three-step DuPont identity shows how profitability, asset efficiency, and financial leverage together drive shareholder returns.
notes: Inputs are decimal ratios, and the result is ROE as a decimal (multiply by 100 for percent). The equity multiplier (assets/equity) captures leverage, so a high ROE may reflect debt rather than operating strength.

name: Extended DuPont (5-Step ROE)
description: Decomposes return on equity into five factors: tax burden, interest burden, operating margin, asset turnover, and the equity multiplier, multiplied together. This extended DuPont breakdown separates the effects of taxes and financing costs from operating performance and leverage.
notes: Tax burden is net income over pretax income, and interest burden is pretax income over EBIT; all inputs are decimals and the result is ROE as a decimal (multiply by 100 for percent).

name: Debt-to-Equity Multiple
description: Computes the debt-to-equity ratio as total debt divided by total equity. It measures financial leverage by showing how much debt financing the firm uses relative to shareholders' equity.
notes: Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities vs. interest-bearing debt only), so keep the numerator consistent. A value of 1 means debt equals equity.

name: Debt-to-Assets Ratio
description: Computes the debt-to-assets ratio as total debt divided by total assets. It indicates the proportion of a company's assets financed by debt, serving as a measure of leverage and solvency risk.
notes: The result is a fraction between 0 and 1 when debt does not exceed assets; a value above 1 signals negative equity. Keep the debt definition consistent with how assets are measured.

name: Equity-to-Assets Ratio
description: Computes the equity-to-assets ratio as total equity divided by total assets. It shows the share of assets funded by owners' equity rather than debt, indicating financial stability and the equity cushion available.
notes: This ratio is the complement of the debt-to-assets ratio when total assets equal debt plus equity, so the two sum to 1. A higher value means lower leverage.

name: Interest Coverage Ratio (Times Interest Earned)
description: Computes the interest coverage ratio (times interest earned) as EBIT divided by interest expense. It measures how many times a company's operating earnings can cover its interest obligations, gauging its ability to service debt.
notes: EBIT is earnings before interest and taxes; a higher ratio means a larger safety margin for interest payments. A value near or below 1 indicates earnings barely cover interest.

name: Debt Service Coverage Ratio
description: Computes the debt service coverage ratio as net operating income divided by total debt service. It measures whether operating income is sufficient to cover required principal and interest payments over a period.
notes: Debt service includes both principal and interest due; a ratio below 1 means income does not fully cover obligations. Lenders often require a minimum such as 1.2 or higher.

name: Net Working Capital
description: Computes net working capital as current assets minus current liabilities. It represents the short-term liquidity available to fund day-to-day operations after covering near-term obligations.
notes: A positive value indicates a liquidity buffer; a negative value can signal short-term funding pressure. This is an absolute currency amount, not a ratio.

name: Margin of Safety Ratio
description: Computes the margin of safety ratio as actual sales minus break-even sales, divided by actual sales. It shows how far sales can fall, as a fraction, before the firm reaches its break-even point and stops making a profit.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent); a larger value means more cushion. Break-even sales must be expressed in the same units as actual sales.

name: Contribution Margin per Unit
description: Computes the contribution margin per unit as selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit. It is the amount each unit sold contributes toward covering fixed costs and then generating profit.
notes: This covers only variable costs; fixed costs are not deducted here. Dividing total fixed costs by this margin gives the break-even quantity in units.

name: Degree of Operating Leverage (Contribution)
description: Computes the degree of operating leverage as total contribution margin divided by operating income (contribution margin minus fixed costs). It measures how sensitively operating income responds to a change in sales volume.
notes: A value of, say, 1.667 means a 1% change in sales produces about a 1.667% change in operating income. The denominator (contribution margin minus fixed costs) must be positive.

name: Degree of Financial Leverage
description: Computes the degree of financial leverage as EBIT divided by EBIT minus interest expense. It measures how sensitively earnings per share (or net income) respond to a change in operating income, reflecting the effect of fixed financing costs.
notes: The denominator is pretax income; the larger the interest expense relative to EBIT, the higher the leverage. If interest equals or exceeds EBIT, the measure breaks down.

name: Degree of Combined Leverage
description: Computes the degree of combined leverage as the product of the degree of operating leverage and the degree of financial leverage. It measures the total sensitivity of earnings per share to a change in sales, combining operating and financial risk.
notes: It equals contribution margin divided by pretax income and captures both cost structure and financing effects. Inputs are the two component leverage factors as decimals.

name: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)
description: Computes the economic order quantity as the square root of two times annual demand times order cost, divided by holding cost per unit. It gives the order size that minimizes total annual ordering plus holding costs.
notes: Assumes steady demand, constant costs, and no shortages; order cost is per order and holding cost is per unit per year. Real order sizes may be rounded to practical batch quantities.

name: EOQ Minimum Total Cost
description: Computes the minimum total annual inventory cost at the economic order quantity as the square root of two times annual demand times order cost times holding cost per unit. At the optimal order size, annual ordering and holding costs are equal and their sum is minimized.
notes: This gives the combined ordering plus holding cost, excluding purchase price of the goods; it uses the same assumptions as the EOQ model. Order cost is per order and holding cost is per unit per year.

name: Reorder Point (with Safety Stock)
description: Computes the reorder point as daily demand times lead time in days, plus safety stock. It is the inventory level at which a new order should be placed so that stock lasts through the replenishment lead time, with a buffer for variability.
notes: Daily demand and lead time must use the same time unit (days); safety stock is added to protect against demand or lead-time variation. The result is in inventory units.

name: Declining-Balance Depreciation (Annual)
description: Computes one year's declining-balance depreciation as the book value at the start of the year multiplied by a fixed depreciation rate. This accelerated method charges more depreciation in early years, applying the same rate to a shrinking book value.
notes: Depreciation is based on book value, not original cost, so the amount falls each year; the rate is entered as a decimal. Depreciation normally stops once book value reaches the salvage value.

name: Double-Declining-Balance Depreciation
description: Computes one year's double-declining-balance depreciation as two divided by the useful life in years, multiplied by the book value at the start of the year. It applies twice the straight-line rate to the current book value, front-loading depreciation.
notes: The rate 2/n is applied to book value, not to the depreciable base, so salvage value is not subtracted in the formula. Depreciation should not reduce book value below salvage value in the final years.

name: Sum-of-the-Years-Digits Depreciation
description: Computes one year's sum-of-the-years-digits depreciation by weighting the depreciable base (cost minus salvage) by the remaining life over the sum of the years' digits, n(n+1)/2. This accelerated method charges more in early years and less later.
notes: The remaining life is measured at the start of the year and decreases by one each year; the depreciable base subtracts salvage value, unlike declining-balance methods. Over the full life the fractions sum to 1.

name: Units-of-Production Depreciation
description: Computes units-of-production depreciation by spreading the depreciable base (cost minus salvage) over total expected output, then multiplying by units produced this period. Depreciation tracks actual usage rather than the passage of time.
notes: The per-unit rate stays constant while the annual charge varies with production; total depreciation over the asset's life equals cost minus salvage. All unit figures must use the same output measure.

name: Book Value (Straight-Line, After t Years)
description: Computes the book value of an asset after t years under straight-line depreciation, subtracting t years of annual depreciation ((cost minus salvage) divided by useful life) from the original cost. It gives the remaining carrying value on the balance sheet.
notes: Valid for t between 0 and the useful life; at the end of the life the book value equals the salvage value. Straight-line assumes an equal depreciation charge each year.

name: Retention (Plowback) Ratio
description: Computes the retention (plowback) ratio as one minus dividends paid divided by net income. It is the fraction of earnings kept in the business rather than distributed to shareholders, funding reinvestment and growth.
notes: It is the complement of the dividend payout ratio, so the two sum to 1; the result is a decimal fraction. Multiplying it by return on equity gives the sustainable growth rate.

name: Altman Z-Score (Manufacturing)
description: Computes the Altman Z-score for manufacturing firms as a weighted sum of five financial ratios: working capital, retained earnings, and EBIT relative to assets, market equity to liabilities, and sales to assets. It is a composite predictor of bankruptcy risk.
notes: For this original model, a score above about 2.99 suggests safety and below about 1.81 signals distress; it applies to public manufacturers, with different coefficients for other firm types.

name: Defensive Interval Ratio
description: Computes the defensive interval ratio as the sum of cash, marketable securities, and receivables divided by daily operating expenses. It estimates how many days a firm can cover its operating costs using only its liquid defensive assets.
notes: The result is a number of days and excludes inventory; daily operating expense is typically annual cash operating costs divided by 365. It ignores any incoming revenue during the period.

name: Capital Intensity Ratio
description: Computes the capital intensity ratio as total assets divided by revenue. It measures how many units of assets are required to generate one unit of sales, indicating how asset-heavy a business is.
notes: It is the reciprocal of total asset turnover, so higher values mean lower asset efficiency. Capital-intensive industries naturally show larger ratios.

name: Return on Net Assets (RONA)
description: Computes return on net assets as net income divided by the sum of fixed assets and net working capital. It measures how efficiently a company generates profit from the capital tied up in operating assets.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Net working capital already nets current liabilities against current assets, so it should not double-count liabilities.

name: Cash Flow Margin
description: Computes the cash flow margin as operating cash flow divided by revenue. It shows how effectively sales are converted into actual operating cash, complementing accrual-based profit margins.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Because it uses cash flow rather than net income, it is less affected by non-cash accounting items like depreciation.

name: Net Debt to EBITDA
description: Computes the net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio as total debt minus cash and equivalents, divided by EBITDA. It measures how many years of current earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization would be needed to repay net debt.
notes: Cash is subtracted to reflect debt that could be repaid immediately; a negative result means cash exceeds debt. Lenders often set covenant limits such as 3x or 4x.

name: Predetermined Overhead Rate
description: Computes the predetermined overhead rate as estimated total overhead divided by the estimated allocation base. It gives the rate used to apply manufacturing overhead to products per unit of the chosen base, such as labor hours or machine hours.
notes: Both figures are estimates set before the period begins; the rate is expressed per unit of the allocation base. Actual overhead may differ, causing over- or under-applied overhead to reconcile later.

name: Cost of Goods Manufactured
description: Computes the cost of goods manufactured as beginning work-in-process inventory plus total manufacturing costs, minus ending work-in-process inventory. It is the total production cost of units completed and transferred to finished goods during the period.
notes: Total manufacturing costs include direct materials, direct labor, and applied overhead. This measures goods finished in the period, which differs from cost of goods sold.

name: Cost of Goods Sold (Periodic)
description: Computes cost of goods sold under the periodic method as beginning inventory plus net purchases, minus ending inventory. It represents the cost of the inventory actually sold during the period.
notes: Beginning inventory plus net purchases equals goods available for sale, from which ending inventory is subtracted. Accuracy depends on a reliable physical count of ending inventory.

name: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
description: Computes the accounting rate of return as average annual profit divided by average investment. It expresses the expected annual accounting profit of a project as a fraction of the capital invested.
notes: It is based on accrual profit and ignores the time value of money, unlike IRR or NPV; the result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Average investment is often taken as (initial + salvage) / 2.

name: Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio
description: Computes the fixed-charge coverage ratio as EBIT plus lease payments, divided by interest expense plus lease payments. It measures a firm's ability to cover fixed financing charges, including both interest and lease obligations.
notes: Lease payments are added back to earnings and included in the charges because they are committed fixed costs; a higher ratio indicates a greater ability to meet obligations. It extends the interest coverage ratio to include leases.
